title: Constructing Written Test Questions For the Basic and Clinical Sciences earchgate.net/publication/242759434_Constructing_Written_Test_Questions_For_the_Basic_and_Clin ical_Sciences
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 10, 2025 — original paper: https://www.res
summary: This entry summarizes Case and Swanson's widely used guide to writing multiple-choice test questions for medical examinations, as covered by Barton. The manual argues that assessment should test application of knowledge through clinically relevant scenarios rather than rote recall, and it catalogs the item-writing flaws that let test-wise students succeed regardless of actual understanding. It works through question formats including one-best-answer and extended-matching items, gives templates and worked examples, and explains how to build patient vignettes using a consistent structure (age, gender, setting, presenting complaint, history, findings, and so on). The guide is explicit that assessment communicates values: what a teacher chooses to test signals to students what actually matters, so test design is itself an act of curriculum communication, not just a measurement tool.
points: Test items should assess application of knowledge through realistic (clinical) vignettes rather than recall of isolated facts — the format should force reasoning, not memorisation.

Distractors need to be homogeneous in length, grammar, and plausibility with the correct answer; true/false and 'none of the above' formats are discouraged because they invite ambiguity or reward test-taking tricks.
Assessment itself communicates what a teacher values — tests aren't neutral measurement, they actively shape what students believe is worth learning.
A mix of assessment methods, frequent short quizzes, and integrative cross-topic tests are all recommended over relying on one infrequent, single-format test.
quotes: It emphasizes assessing application of knowledge rather than rote memorization, advocating for clinically relevant scenarios and avoiding flawed question structures that benefit test-wise students.
A primary purpose of testing is to communicate what you view as important. Tests are a powerful motivator, and students will learn what they believe you value

Teachers should be aware of technical item flaws related to testwiseness (e.g., grammatical or logical cues, long correct answers) and irrelevant difficulty (e.g., long, complicated, or double options, vague frequency terms).
All distractors should be homogeneous, plausible, grammatically consistent, logically compatible, and of the same length as the correct answer.

Teachers should avoid using true/false questions because they often lead to ambiguity and assess recall of isolated facts. One-best-answer questions are better for assessing application of knowledge, integration, synthesis, and judgement.
Teachers should consider using frequent short quizzes rather than infrequent tests.
